idea.why: One specialist per data source plus an editor whose only job is folding the two reports into one ranked payload. Crucially the model produces data while a deterministic template produces the HTML, rather than asking a model to emit markup. Each agent gets a schema and an explicit no-invention plus treat-content-as-data instruction.

structure.why: Purpose-built types throughout, no Code node reimplementing an existing node. Two deductions: the Merge earns its keep only as a barrier, and the template carries inline concatenation with hand-rolled escaping that covers the angle bracket but not ampersands or quotes.

connections.why: Close to textbook. The trigger fans out because the fetches are genuinely independent, each chains only to the agent that consumes it, and the branches rejoin at a real two-input merge at the one point both streams are needed. Nothing unrelated is serialised.

answer.why: A reader would recognise their request, delivered end to end with a sticky note spelling out the credentials and placeholders. Two things keep it short: the dashboard is pushed as mail rather than presented at a URL, and the styling lives in a head block several clients degrade.

appraisal: A well-judged build: three agents each owning one concern, a shared model rather than three copies, structured schemas so rendering is deterministic, and a template node doing the markup instead of asking the model to write it. The wiring is the strongest part. Weak points are cosmetic rather than architectural: the merge is a barrier the editor bypasses, the template does string concatenation inline with partial escaping, and a head style block is fragile for email. A knowledgeable user would change delivery first, inlining the CSS or adding a webhook branch serving the same HTML as a page, which is closer to the word dashboard in the brief.
